newsitem.title: UK: CRICKET-LAMB CONSIDERING APPEAL AGAINST LIBEL CASE.
newsitem.headline: CRICKET-LAMB CONSIDERING APPEAL AGAINST LIBEL CASE.

text.p: Former England batsman Allan Lamb, who lost a libel action against former Pakistan captain Imran Khan in the High Court on July 31, is seriously considering an appeal.

Lamb and Ian Botham, his team mate in the England side during the 1980s and early 1990s, took Imran to court over what they described as an "offensive personal attack" on them in India Today magazine which they said called them racist and uneducated.
Imran said the words had been taken out of context.
"No decision has been made and there's not much more time to make a decision," Lamb's solicitor Alan Herd said on Thursday.
"But you can definitely say he is seriously considering an appeal."
Herd dismissed reports that Lamb and Botham had been left with a legal bill of 500,000 pounds sterling ($784,600) between them, saying the actual figure was "less than half of that".
Lamb, speaking at the launch at his autobiography, said he was still shocked at the verdict.
"It's made a fairly big hole in my pocket," he said. "It's taken me on the chin a bit but it's something you've just got to get up from.
"I know how the case should have gone; I think 80 percent of the British public know which way it should have gone."

South African-born Lamb, who played 79 tests for England and scored over 30,000 first class runs, also said he was appalled by officials' decision to forbid a book-signing session at Lord's during the NatWest Trophy final this weekend.
He said he still felt let down by the English cricket authorities over the ball-tampering row which he first brought to prominence four years ago.
"I feel I stood up for the players and the game. I'm afraid I didn't get the support of my own board. Too many people stayed on the fence," Lamb said.
